Section 208 (1341/2014)
Notifying the Non-Discrimination Ombudsman

The Non-Discrimination Ombudsman shall be notified of any decision under this Act to issue a
residence permit on the basis of international or temporary protection, to deny admittance or stay
to an alien, or to refuse entry to or deport an alien. The Non-Discrimination Ombudsman shall also
be notified without delay of any decision concerning detention of an alien or a child’s residence
obligation. At the request of the Non-Discrimination Ombudsman, the Ombudsman shall also be
notified of any other decisions under this Act and the necessary information required for
overseeing the enforcement of removals from the country under section 152b. (49/2017)

Provisions on the right of the Non-Discrimination Ombudsman to obtain information are laid down
in section 4 of the Act on the Non-Discrimination Ombudsman (1326/2014).

Section 209 (1341/2014)
Hearing the views of the Non-Discrimination Ombudsman

Provisions on the right of the Non-Discrimination Ombudsman to obtain information are laid down
in section 4 of the Act on the Non-Discrimination Ombudsman (1326/2014).

Section 209 (1341/2014)
Hearing the views of the Non-Discrimination Ombudsman

At the request of the Non-Discrimination Ombudsman, the Ombudsman has the right to be heard
in an individual matter concerning an asylum applicant or deportation of an alien. The authority
deciding on the matter may, on a case-by-case basis, set a reasonable time limit for the issue of a
statement by the Non-Discrimination Ombudsman.

Section 210 (886/2011)

Right of the Finnish Immigration Service to decide on matters falling within the
competence of local police departments

The Finnish Immigration Service may take up a matter for decision which, under this Act, is to be
decided by the local police department.

The local police department may refer a matter falling within its competence to the Finnish
Immigration Service for decision if the examination of the matter and any decisions on the matter
require the expertise of the Finnish Immigration Service because of the nature of the matter, or if
the matter is important for the application of the law to other similar cases.

Section 211 (554/2021)
Advisory Board for Terms of Employment and Permit Supervision of Foreign Workers
and Entrepreneurs

Section 211 (554/2021)
Advisory Board for Terms of Employment and Permit Supervision of Foreign Workers
and Entrepreneurs

For the purpose of supervising the terms of employment of foreign labour, an Advisory Board for
Terms of Employment and Permit Supervision of Foreign Workers and Entrepreneurs may be
appointed in connection with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment. The task of the
Board is to promote cooperation and communication between the authorities in matters pertaining
to the supervision of the terms of employment of foreign workers and supervision of residence
permits for employed persons and entrepreneurs, to monitor trends in the supervision of the terms
of employment and residence permits of foreign workers and entrepreneurs and to issue
statements on these matters.

The members of the Advisory Board are appointed by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and
Employment. The authorities and administrative branches involved in the supervision shall be
represented in the Advisory Board. The Advisory Board cooperates with key labour market
organisations and industrial policy organisations.

Further provisions on the Advisory Board’s composition, duties, work procedures and term of office
are given by government decree.

provisions of this Act and any provisions issued under it. (973/2007)

Section 214
Entry into force

This Act enters into force on 1 May 2004.

This Act repeals the Aliens Act of 22 February 1991 (378/1991), as amended.

Section 215
Transitional provisions

The provisions in force at the time of the entry into force of this Act apply to matters that are
pending at that time. However, the provisions of this Act apply to matters returned for
reconsideration.

Matters related to a residence permit pending at the time of the entry into force of this Act will
lapse if no residence permit is needed under this Act in the cases concerned.

Matters related to a residence permit pending at the time of the entry into force of this Act will

The requirement concerning a period of residence of four years laid down in section 56 is applied

force at the time of the entry into force of this Act apply if residence of continuous nature has

What benefits can you get from Kela?
Kela can pay benefits in many different life situations.
You can get benefits if you cannot work for instance
because you have small children, you are ill or
you study.
The benefits Kela can pay are defined in Finnish law.
Benefits paid by Kela include for instance
• national pension, guarantee pension
and other benefits for pensioners
• general housing allowance
• reimbursements for medicine costs
• other benefits in case of illness
• unemployment benefits
• financial aid for students
• benefits for families.
Kela card
Kela issues a Kela card to everyone who has the right to
get reimbursements for medicine costs or
other illness-related benefits.
If you have a Kela card and you go to a private medical clinic
for treatment, you can often get reimbursement for
the costs of your treatment right away by
showing your Kela card at the clinic.
This way you do not have to apply for reimbursement
afterwards.
The Kela card is free of charge,
and Kela sends it to your home address.
Who can get Kela benefits?
You can usually get benefits from Kela
in the following situations:
• You live in Finland permanently.
• You work in Finland and you earn at least
about EUR 800 per month in salary or wages.
An exception to this is if you live in Finland but
you work in another EU country.
In that case, you can usually not get benefits from Kela.
What does it mean to
live permanently in a country?
You live in Finland permanently if

about EUR 800 per month in salary or wages.
An exception to this is if you live in Finland but
you work in another EU country.
In that case, you can usually not get benefits from Kela.
What does it mean to
live permanently in a country?
You live in Finland permanently if
your main residence and home is here.
You must also stay in Finland for
at least 6 months of the year.
When you move to Finland, Kela will check if
your move can be considered permanent.
Your overall situation is considered,
and it is affected by, for example, the following factors:
• You have lived in Finland before.
• The duration of your employment contract if
you come to Finland to work.
• Your partner or some other close relative
lives in Finland permanently.
If you move to Finland temporarily, you do not usually
have the right to Kela benefits.
For example, asylum seekers do not have the right to
Kela benefits.

When you move to Finland
The conditions you have to meet to get Kela benefits are
different depending on if you move to Finland as
• a worker or a self-employed person
• a posted worker
• an accompanying family member
• a student
• a pensioner.
If you have a municipality of residence (kotikunta) in Finland,
you can use public healthcare services.
Your local municipal health centre is usually the first place
you should go for treatment.
If you do not have a municipality of residence, ask Kela to
check if you have the right to use public healthcare services.
Benefits for employees
and self-employed persons
You can get some benefits from Kela if you work in Finland.
Examples of these benefits are sickness allowance
and the child benefit.
You have the right to get benefits from Kela in the months
when you earn at least about EUR 800 by working.
If you work in Finland for at least 6 months,
you may have the right to certain Kela benefits
even after you have stopped working.
If you are a worker, you also have the right to
occupational health services.
Ask your employer for more information.
8
9
When you move to Finland,
your life situation will affect what
Kela benefits you can get.

Posted workers
Posted workers are persons that a foreign employer has
sent to work in Finland.
If you come to Finland as a posted worker from
another EU or EEA country or from Switzerland
or the United Kingdom, you are covered by
the social security system of the country you came from.
In such case, you do not have the right to Kela benefits.
You need a certificate A1 from the country you were sent from.
If you come as a posted worker from a country that has
signed a social security agreement with Finland,
ask Kela to check if you can get Kela benefits.
The agreements Finland has signed with different countries
differ from each other.
Kela benefits if you do not work in Finland
Family members
If you move to Finland as the family member of
an employee or a student, you will usually have to
live in Finland permanently to qualify for Kela benefits.
Students
If you move to Finland from a country that is not
an EU or EEA country, Switzerland or the United Kingdom
solely to study in Finland, you can get some
Kela benefits, such as sickness allowance and
daily allowances for parents.
Your studies must last for at least 2 years for you to qualify.

However, you may not have the right to all Kela benefits,
such as student financial aid, housing allowance or
the maternity grant.
Students who come to Finland from another EU country
usually do not have the right to Kela benefits.
You may have the right to Kela benefits if
you also work in Finland in addition to studying.
But even in that case, you will usually not qualify for
student financial aid.
If you come to Finland to complete a higher education degree,
you can use the healthcare services provided by
the Finnish Student Health Service (FSHS).
Pensioners
If you move to Finland as a pensioner,
you must live in Finland permanently
to qualify for Kela benefits.
When can you get Kela benefits?
You usually qualify for Kela benefits
starting from the day you move to Finland or
start working in Finland.
However, Kela pays some benefits only to persons who
have lived in Finland for a certain period of time
before they are granted the benefit.
Examples of these benefits are
• pensions paid by Kela
• disability allowance for persons who are over 16 years old.
When checking if you can get certain benefits,
Kela will take into consideration periods
you have lived or worked in another EU or EEA country,
Switzerland or the United Kingdom.

10

Example: Rachel moves to Finland
for work
Rachel moves to Finland from the United States to
work for a Finnish company.
When she arrives, Rachel tells Kela that she will live in
Finland only for a few months.
Because this is a short, temporary stay,
she does not qualify for Kela benefits that are
granted on the basis of residency.
However, because Rachel came to Finland to work, she
qualifies for certain Kela benefits that are granted based
on employment immediately after she starts working.
Kela will pay these benefits to her if she meets
the other conditions that apply to them.
These benefits include, for example, reimbursements for
medical expenses and sickness allowance.
Later Rachel’s employment is made permanent.
Rachel’s temporary stay in Finland turns into permanent
residence.
This means that she now lives in Finland permanently.
After this, Rachel also has the right to benefits that are
only paid to persons who live in Finland permanently.
These benefits include, for example, housing allowance
and the maternity grant.
Example: Amila moves to Finland
to study
Amila moves to Finland from Sri Lanka.
Amila starts a course of study at
a university of applied sciences.
Amila’s studies last for 4 years.
This means that she qualifies for some Kela benefits.
For example, Amila can get sickness allowance.
However, Amila does not qualify for student financial aid
or housing benefits.
